nameStory: The name 'yellow devil' comes from this hawkweed's bright yellow flowers and its reputation as a troublesome weed that spreads aggressively. Like other hawkweeds, it was thought to improve the eyesight of hawks who ate it, giving the whole group its common name. The 'devil' part reflects how gardeners and farmers feel when they try to remove this persistent plant!
description: Yellow-devil is a low-growing perennial wildflower in the daisy family that forms spreading patches through underground runners. It produces clusters of bright yellow, dandelion-like flower heads on stems that reach 1-2 feet tall. The plant has a rosette of fuzzy, pale green leaves at its base and is considered an invasive species that can quickly take over lawns and meadows. Originally from Europe, it's now established across much of North America.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads that look like small dandelions, clustered together at the top of branching stems. Each flower head has only ray petals (the petal-like parts) with square-toothed tips, giving them a fringed appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Pale green, oval-shaped leaves covered in soft, whitish hairs that feel fuzzy to the touch. Most leaves form a low rosette at the base of the plant, with few or no leaves on the flowering stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense patches through creeping underground stems called stolons. Individual plants stay low to the ground except for the 1-2 foot tall flowering stems that emerge from the leaf rosettes.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds with white, fluffy parachutes (like dandelion seeds) that blow away in the wind. The seeds are dark brown and about 1/8 inch long.

habitat: Yellow-devil thrives in disturbed areas like roadsides, old fields, and lawn edges, preferring well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade. It's commonly found in areas with poor or sandy soil where other plants struggle to compete. Look for it in meadows, pastures, and anywhere the ground has been disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from overwintering rosettes, appearing pale green and very fuzzy. Flower buds begin forming on emerging stems in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flower clusters most visible from June through August. Seeds with fluffy white parachutes disperse in late summer breezes.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may persist but become less noticeable as flowering stops. Plants focus energy on spreading through underground runners.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back, but some basal leaves may persist in milder areas. Underground portions remain alive and ready to sprout in spring.

funFact: Yellow-devil can reproduce both by seeds and by sending out underground runners, but here's the twist: many hawkweed populations are actually clones that produce seeds without fertilization, meaning entire patches might be genetically identical copies of a single 'mother' plant!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with orange hawkweed (devil's paintbrush), but yellow-devil has bright yellow flowers instead of orange-red ones. Also similar to dandelions, but dandelions have deeply toothed leaves and single flowers on hollow stems, while yellow-devil has fuzzy, smooth-edged leaves and multiple flower heads clustered together.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is considered a noxious weed in many areas and is banned or restricted in some states due to its aggressive spreading habit. Despite being called 'yellow devil hawkweed' sometimes, it's actually a different species from Yellow Devil Hawkweed (Pilosella glomerata), which can cause naming confusion.
compareHints: Yellow-devil differs from orange hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and generally paler, more silvery-fuzzy leaves. Unlike mouse-eared hawkweed which has solitary flower heads, yellow-devil produces clusters of multiple flower heads together. It's also typically more robust and forms denser patches than its close relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orange hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctive orange-red flowers—most other hawkweeds in New England have yellow blooms.
Mouse-eared hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctively fuzzy, silvery leaves and single yellow flowers on leafless stems.
Meadow hawkweed differs from its orange hawkweed cousin by having yellow flowers instead of orange-red ones.
Smooth hawkweed towers above its mouse-eared hawkweed cousin, which stays close to the ground in creeping mats with densely fuzzy leaves.
Yellow Devil differs from Orange Hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and more tightly clustered flower heads.
